hints: Think about how phenol behaves as a weak acid toward a reactive metal, in the same way as water or an alcohol does.
walkthrough:
Spot the acidic proton**
Phenol has an $\text{O-H}$ group attached directly to the benzene ring. That proton is weakly acidic, so a strong reducing metal like sodium will remove it, just as sodium does with water or ethanol.

Write the salt plus hydrogen**
The $\text{H}$ of the $\text{OH}$ is replaced by $\text{Na}$ to give sodium phenoxide, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa}$, and hydrogen gas is released: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2$$ Balance the $\text{H}_2$ with $\tfrac{1}{2}$ or double the whole equation.

hints: Recall that the $\text{OH}$ group strongly activates the benzene ring and directs incoming electrophiles to specific positions.
walkthrough:
Remember how activating phenol is**
The lone pair on the $\text{OH}$ oxygen is donated into the ring, making phenol far more reactive than benzene. Even dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ is enough to nitrate it, with no concentrated acid catalyst needed.

Place the nitro groups ortho and para**
The $\text{OH}$ group is 2,4-directing. So electrophilic substitution puts $\text{NO}_2$ ortho to $\text{OH}$ to give 2-nitrophenol, and para to $\text{OH}$ to give 4-nitrophenol. Draw both isomers with the benzene ring, $\text{OH}$ retained, and one $\text{NO}_2$ in the 2-position and one in the 4-position.
Final answer: Two mononitration products: 2-nitrophenol (benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and ortho $\text{NO}_2$) and 4-nitrophenol (benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and para $\text{NO}_2$).

hints: Start by deciding which species is electron rich and which is electron poor, look closely at the $\text{C=O}$ bonds in $\text{CO}_2$.
Recall the general two stage pattern for electrophilic substitution on a benzene ring: attack to break aromaticity, then restore aromaticity by losing $\text{H}^+$.
Think about what the ring looks like just after the new $\text{C-C}$ bond forms but before aromaticity is restored, and where the $\text{H}^+$ comes from in the second step.
walkthrough:
Make CO2 an electrophile**
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so each $\text{C=O}$ is polarised $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$. Label those dipoles. The phenoxide ring is very electron rich because of the $\text{O}^-$ group, so it is the nucleophile that will attack the $\delta^+$ carbon.

Form the first C-C bond**
Draw a curly arrow starting inside the benzene hexagon, representing the pi electrons, and pointing to the $\text{C}$ atom of $\text{CO}_2$. At the same time a pair from one $\text{C=O}$ moves onto oxygen. This is electrophilic attack at the ortho position, which leads toward salicylic acid.

Draw the Wheland type intermediate**
After attack, aromaticity is temporarily lost. Draw a six membered ring with two double bonds and a positive charge delocalised, still bearing the $\text{O}^-$ substituent, plus the attacked carbon now tetrahedral with both H and the new $\text{C}(\text{OO}^-)$ group attached. This is the organic intermediate in the box.

Restore aromaticity**
Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond on that tetrahedral carbon back into the ring to reform the pi system. The $\text{H}$ leaves as $\text{H}^+$. That gives the ortho substituted product ion with $\text{COO}^-$ and $\text{O}^-$ groups, which on acidification gives salicylic acid.

Final answer: Show $\delta^+$ on C and $\delta^-$ on O of $\text{C=O}$ in $\text{CO}_2$ with curly arrow from inside benzene ring of $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ to $\delta^+$ C.
Intermediate: cyclohexadienyl cation type structure with $\text{O}^-$ retained, new $\text{COO}^-$ group and H on the attacked ortho carbon, positive charge delocalised in ring.
Curly arrow from $\text{C-H}$ bond back into ring to reform aromatic system + $\text{H}^+$ lost.

hints: Visualise the Diels-Alder as three pi bonds moving in a circle at the same time to make one new pi bond and two new sigma bonds.
walkthrough:
Follow the circle of electrons**
This is a concerted reaction, all bonds change together. Draw one curly arrow from the ethene pi bond to meet one end of the diene, a second curly arrow from one diene double bond to meet the other end of ethene, and a third curly arrow from the other diene double bond shifting to the centre to form the new double bond in cyclohexene. All three arrows point round in the same cyclic direction.

Final answer: Three concerted curly arrows: from $\text{C=C}$ of ethene to form new sigma bond, and from the two $\text{C=C}$ bonds of buta-1,3-diene to form one new sigma bond and the new $\text{C=C}$ in cyclohexene, giving cyclohexene.

hints: Treat the $\text{C=C}$ in the five membered ring as ethene, the two ends of buta-1,3-diene join across it to build a new six membered ring fused to it.
walkthrough:
Fuse the diene onto the cyclopentene double bond**
Keep the five membered ring and its methyl group unchanged. The butadiene adds across the $\text{C=C}$ of 3-methylcyclopentene. Join C1 of the diene to one alkene carbon and C4 of the diene to the other alkene carbon, forming a new six membered ring sharing that bond. Put one double bond in the middle of the newly added four carbon bridge. That gives a fused 6,5 bicyclic system with the methyl still on the five membered part.

Final answer: Fused bicyclic adduct: new six-membered ring with one $\text{C=C}$ fused across the original double bond of 3-methylcyclopentene, retaining the methyl substituent on the five-membered ring.
